subject: Neurology
vignette: A 24-year-old man has episodes in which he suddenly smells burnt rubber, then experiences involuntary rhythmic jerking of his right hand for 30 seconds. He remains fully conscious and aware during the episode and can describe it afterward.
question: Which seizure type best fits this episode?
explanation_correct: Focal seizures originate in a single area of the brain, most commonly the medial temporal lobe. A focal aware seizure, formerly called a simple partial seizure, preserves consciousness and may feature motor, sensory, autonomic, or psychic symptoms such as an olfactory aura of burnt rubber followed by focal motor jerking. The aura is the early part of a seizure. Because awareness remains intact, this is focal aware rather than focal impaired awareness.

explanation_incorrect.A: Focal impaired awareness seizures involve impaired consciousness and automatisms; this patient remains fully aware and can describe the event afterward.
explanation_incorrect.B: A generalized tonic-clonic seizure involves bilateral stiffening and movements with loss of consciousness and a postictal phase, not a focal aware sensory and motor spell.
explanation_incorrect.D: Absence seizures are brief blank stares with 3 Hz spike-and-wave and no aura or focal motor jerking, and they occur mainly in children.
explanation_incorrect.E: Atonic seizures are drop seizures with sudden loss of postural tone and falls, not an aura with focal jerking and preserved awareness.

educationalObjective: Focal aware seizures preserve consciousness and can begin with an aura such as an olfactory hallucination before focal motor symptoms.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 7-year-old girl has multiple brief daily episodes of blank staring lasting about 10 seconds, during which she is unresponsive but does not fall or convulse. She returns immediately to her prior activity with no confusion. Hyperventilation triggers the episodes, and EEG shows 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges.
question: Which seizure type best fits these episodes?
explanation_correct: Absence (petit mal) seizures feature 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges on EEG, short episodes of blank stare usually lasting about 10 seconds, possible automatisms, and no postictal confusion. They can be triggered by hyperventilation and are common in children. The immediate return to baseline without postictal confusion is characteristic.

explanation_incorrect.A: Myoclonic seizures are quick, repetitive jerks without loss of consciousness and are not associated with blank staring and 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges.
explanation_incorrect.B: Tonic-clonic (grand mal) seizures involve alternating stiffening and movement followed by postictal confusion, incontinence, and tongue biting, all absent here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Focal impaired awareness seizures involve impaired consciousness with automatisms and a postictal phase, not the 3 Hz spike-and-wave blank stares of absence seizures.
explanation_incorrect.E: Tonic seizures consist of sustained stiffening without the blank stare and 3 Hz spike-and-wave pattern described in this patient.

educationalObjective: Absence seizures cause brief blank stares with 3 Hz spike-and-wave EEG, no postictal confusion, and precipitation by hyperventilation.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 19-year-old man has a generalized seizure in which he initially stiffens and then has rhythmic jerking of all four limbs for about 90 seconds. Afterward he is confused and lethargic for an hour, is incontinent of urine, and has bitten his tongue.
question: Which seizure type best matches this episode?
explanation_correct: Generalized tonic-clonic (grand mal) seizures consist of alternating stiffening (the tonic phase) and rhythmic movements (the clonic phase) with loss of consciousness. They are followed by a postictal period of confusion and commonly feature urinary incontinence and tongue biting. The prolonged postictal state and tongue biting distinguish this from absence and myoclonic seizures.

explanation_incorrect.A: Absence seizures are brief blank stares with 3 Hz spike-and-wave and no postictal confusion, incontinence, or tongue biting.
explanation_incorrect.C: Myoclonic seizures are quick repetitive jerks without loss of consciousness or postictal confusion, not a tonic-clonic sequence with a prolonged postictal state.
explanation_incorrect.D: Atonic (drop) seizures cause sudden loss of tone and falls, not tonic stiffening followed by clonic jerking with a postictal phase.
explanation_incorrect.E: A focal aware seizure preserves consciousness and lacks the bilateral convulsions, incontinence, and postictal confusion described in this patient.

educationalObjective: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures feature a tonic then clonic phase with loss of consciousness and a postictal state with confusion, incontinence, and tongue biting.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A clinician is reviewing three seizure types. One patient has sudden, brief, repetitive muscle jerks without loss of awareness. A second has sudden loss of postural tone and falls to the floor, often mistaken for fainting. A third has sustained stiffening of the limbs.
question: Which option correctly matches each seizure type to its description?

options.text: Myoclonic = stiffening; atonic = jerks; tonic = drop seizures
Myoclonic = drop seizures; tonic = jerks; atonic = stiffening
Tonic = jerks; myoclonic = stiffening; atonic = drop seizures
Myoclonic = quick repetitive jerks; atonic = drop seizures; tonic = stiffening
Atonic = stiffening; tonic = drop seizures; myoclonic = quick repetitive jerks

explanation_correct: Myoclonic seizures are quick, repetitive jerks without loss of consciousness or postictal confusion. Atonic (drop) seizures are sudden loss of postural tone causing falls, commonly mistaken for fainting. Tonic seizures consist of sustained stiffening. Correctly matching these requires recognizing that jerking corresponds to myoclonic, falling to atonic, and stiffening to tonic.

explanation_incorrect.A: Myoclonic seizures are jerks rather than stiffening, and atonic seizures are drop seizures rather than jerks; the assignments are scrambled.
explanation_incorrect.B: Myoclonic seizures are not drop seizures; atonic seizures are the drop seizures, and tonic seizures are stiffening rather than jerks.
explanation_incorrect.C: Tonic seizures are stiffening rather than jerks, and myoclonic seizures are jerks rather than stiffening; the first two assignments are reversed.
explanation_incorrect.E: Atonic seizures are drop seizures, not stiffening, and tonic seizures are stiffening, not drop seizures; these two assignments are swapped.

educationalObjective: Myoclonic seizures are quick jerks, atonic seizures are drop attacks, and tonic seizures are sustained stiffening.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 32-year-old woman has a prolonged episode of shaking resembling a tonic-clonic seizure lasting 3 minutes, witnessed by family, with vocalizations and an apparent aura. There is no postictal confusion, no tongue biting, and no incontinence. Video EEG during the event shows no epileptiform activity. She has a history of depression.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Psychogenic nonepileptic events resemble prolonged, greater than 1 minute, syncopal or tonic-clonic episodes but lack a postictal phase, autonomic disturbances, and tongue biting. They are often witnessed with vocalizations and a preceding aura, show female predominance, and are associated with psychiatric history or substance use. A normal video EEG during the event is the key discriminator.

explanation_incorrect.A: Convulsive status epilepticus is continuous for at least 5 minutes or recurring without return to baseline consciousness and can cause brain injury; this event is shorter with a normal EEG.
explanation_incorrect.B: Epilepsy is a disorder of recurrent unprovoked seizures; a normal ictal video EEG and absent postictal features argue against an epileptic seizure.
explanation_incorrect.C: A generalized tonic-clonic seizure would show epileptiform activity on EEG and typically has postictal confusion, incontinence, and tongue biting, none of which are present here.
explanation_incorrect.D: A focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure would also show epileptiform discharges on video EEG and a postictal state; this event has a normal EEG.

educationalObjective: Psychogenic nonepileptic events mimic prolonged seizures but lack postictal features and tongue biting and show a normal video EEG, often with psychiatric risk factors.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 72-year-old man presents with a first-time seizure and a focal lesion on CT. The clinician notes that the most common causes of seizures in this age group differ from those in children.
question: Which of the following best lists the most common causes of seizures in adults older than 65?

options.text: Genetic, infection (febrile), trauma, congenital, and metabolic causes
Genetic and congenital causes predominate in this age group
Febrile illness and metabolic causes are the only considerations
Stroke, tumor, trauma, metabolic, and infection

explanation_correct: Causes of seizures vary by age. In adults older than 65, the most common causes are stroke, tumor, trauma, metabolic disturbances, and infection. By contrast, children younger than 18 more often have genetic, infection (febrile), trauma, congenital, and metabolic causes, while adults 18-65 have tumor, trauma, stroke, and infection. This age-based pattern guides the evaluation of a first-time seizure.

explanation_incorrect.A: Genetic, febrile infection, trauma, congenital, and metabolic causes are the listed causes for children younger than 18, not adults older than 65.
explanation_incorrect.B: Tumor, trauma, stroke, and infection are the listed causes for adults 18-65; in older adults, metabolic causes and stroke are especially prominent.
explanation_incorrect.C: Genetic and congenital causes are characteristic of younger patients, while older adults are dominated by structural and metabolic causes.
explanation_incorrect.D: Although metabolic causes and infection are relevant, limiting the causes to these two ignores the major structural causes of stroke, tumor, and trauma in older adults.

educationalObjective: In adults older than 65, seizures are most often caused by stroke, tumor, trauma, metabolic disturbances, or infection.
